reading.delprov: Delprov B1a: reading – Volunteer with Us
reading.title: Volunteer with Us
reading.ingress: The texts below are from a website that helps people aged 14–20 find volunteering in the city of Ravensbridge. Use the information in the texts when you answer the questions. Your answers must be in English.

sections.heading: A · Hollow Lane Animal Shelter
paragraphs: We look after around ninety cats and dogs at any one time, and we could not do it without volunteers. Everyone starts in the laundry and the food store – unglamorous, but it is where the work actually is. After three months there you may apply to work directly with the animals.

Minimum age 16. Two four-hour shifts a month. No experience needed, but you must be able to commit for at least six months. Training takes place on the last Saturday of every month; you cannot start without it.

sections.heading: B · The Ravensbridge Story Archive
paragraphs: We record older residents talking about their lives and keep the recordings for the city library. Volunteers do the interviews, and we teach you how: how to ask a question and then say nothing, which is the hardest part.

Age 15 and over. You choose your own hours, but each interview takes about two hours plus travel. Ideal if you like listening more than talking, and we ask you to stay with us for at least ten interviews. Some of our volunteers have been doing this for eleven years.

sections.heading: C · Fieldgate Community Garden
paragraphs: Two acres behind the station, growing vegetables for anyone who needs them. Saturday mornings, March to October, whatever the weather. Boots and gloves provided; bring your own water.

All ages welcome, but under-16s must come with an adult. Just turn up – there is no form to fill in and nobody will ask you to sign anything. We start at nine and there is soup at twelve. Come once or come every Saturday – there is no minimum period.

sections.heading: D · Radio Ravensbridge
paragraphs: Our youth programme is made entirely by people under twenty. Volunteers write, record and edit, and two of our presenters have gone on to work in national radio.

You must be at least 14. The first step is a taster evening in September, and places are limited to twelve. If you are offered a place you commit to one evening a week for a full year. We ask a lot, but you will leave able to do something few people your age can.

sections.heading: E · The Sunday Kitchen
paragraphs: Every Sunday we cook and serve about two hundred meals for anyone who wants one. Volunteers chop, wash up and – most importantly – sit down and eat with the guests.
Age 16 and over for the kitchen, 14 and over for the dining room. Turn up at eight in the morning or at one in the afternoon. Wear clothes you do not mind ruining, and tie your hair back.

sections.heading: F · Bridgehouse Museum
paragraphs: Our young guides run tours for primary school classes. You are given a script for your first term, but after that most guides write their own, and the best tours here have all been invented by teenagers.
From age 15. Tours take place on weekday afternoons, so you need to be free after school. Training is spread over four evenings in August, and you must attend all four before you can guide.

paragraphs: Each explanation describes one word. Choose the word from the alternatives that matches the explanation exactly.
Example: A tool used for cutting, for example hair or paper.  →  scissors

reading.delprov: Delprov B1c: reading – The Last Picture House
reading.title: The Last Picture House

image.alt: An old cinema with red seats.

reading.ingress: This story is about what happened in the small town of Bellmoor in the autumn of 1998. Read the four parts of the story and answer the questions after each part. Your answers must be in English. When answering questions with alternatives – choose one alternative only.

paragraphs: The Regal had been closed for eleven months when Priya first got inside. The door at the back, the one the projectionists had used, had a lock that had given up long before the cinema did, and on the second Saturday of September she pushed it with her shoulder and it opened.

Inside, the air was cold and smelled of dust and, faintly, of oranges. Four hundred and twelve red seats sloped down towards a screen that somebody had covered with a sheet, as if the building were a piece of furniture in a house nobody lived in any more.
She was sixteen and she had seen thirty-one films in that room. She could have told you what she had watched from each of the seats in row K.
Her father said the town had stopped going, and that was that. Her mother said the town had stopped going because there had been nothing worth going to, which was a different thing entirely.

The town council had agreed to sell the building in March. There were two offers: a supermarket chain that wanted to knock it down, and a man from Leeds who had not said what he wanted it for. The decision was to be made at a meeting on the fourth of November.

Priya was not allowed to speak at council meetings, and she knew it. What she was allowed to do, it turned out, was write to every person on the council, which she did — eleven letters, all different, because her English teacher had told her once that eleven identical letters are worth one letter.

Only one councillor replied. Mrs Adeyemi wrote three lines: that she agreed with Priya, that she would be voting against the supermarket, and that one vote out of eleven was not going to be enough, so what else did Priya plan to do?
Priya had not planned anything else. She was, she said later, extremely annoyed to discover that this was a fair question.

What they did next was not clever, and it worked. On the third Saturday in October they showed a film in the Regal without permission — an old projector borrowed from the school, a sheet from Priya's house, and a print of a comedy that Mrs Adeyemi's nephew had somewhere in a garage.

They told nobody except by word of mouth. Two hundred and six people came. The oldest was ninety-one and had been to the Regal on its opening night in 1937; the youngest was four and slept through most of it.

The projector broke twice. Both times somebody in the audience shouted a joke into the dark, and both times the whole room laughed, and Priya understood something that she has never been able to explain properly since: that the film had almost nothing to do with it.

A photographer from the county newspaper had come because he lived three streets away and was curious. The picture he took — two hundred people in a building that was supposed to be finished — was on the front page on the Monday.

The council met on the fourth of November as planned. The supermarket offer was withdrawn a week before the meeting; the chain's regional manager said, in a statement that has been quoted in Bellmoor ever since, that they had reconsidered the location.

The man from Leeds turned out to want to run it as a cinema, which nobody had thought to ask him. He reopened the Regal in April 1999 with two hundred and eighty seats instead of four hundred and twelve, because the back rows had rotted through.

Priya is forty-three now. She does not live in Bellmoor and has not for twenty years. The Regal is still open; it survived a fire in 2011 and a bad decade after that, largely because eight hundred people in a town of nine thousand pay four pounds a month to keep it alive.

She was asked, at the evening marking twenty-five years since the reopening, what she had learned at sixteen. She said she had learned that the building was never the point either, and that it had taken her until roughly the age of thirty to work out what she had meant by that.

listening.title: On Air

image.alt: A microphone in a radio studio.

listening.intro: Du kommer att höra en intervju med Tessa Iyer, som driver en ungdomsradiostation. Läs frågorna först. Dina svar ska vara på engelska, och du får skriva medan du lyssnar.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Welcome back. With me in the studio is Tessa Iyer, who runs Northgate Youth Radio – a station where everything you hear is made by people under twenty-one. Tessa, thanks for coming in.

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: Thanks for having me.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: You started this eight years ago. What were you doing before?

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: I was a librarian, believe it or not, at a school about two miles from where the studio is now. I did that for six years and I was reasonably good at it, but I kept noticing the same thing: the students who had the most to say were often the ones who said the least in class.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: And the station came out of that?

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: It came out of a broken cupboard, really. The school was throwing out some old recording equipment. I asked if I could keep it, and four of us started making a half-hour programme in an empty classroom on Thursday evenings. That was 2017. Nobody listened. I mean that literally – for the first four months our audience was eleven people, and I knew nine of them.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: What changed?

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: We stopped trying to sound like the radio we'd grown up with. Once we did that, everything got better. Now we reach about nineteen thousand listeners a month, which still surprises me.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Who can join?

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: Anyone between fourteen and twenty-one who lives in the county. We take twenty new people each September. You don't need experience, you don't need to be confident, and you definitely don't need what people think of as a radio voice – we have deliberately moved away from that.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Is there anything you do need?

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: Three things, and we're honest about them from the first day. You need to turn up, because a programme that is half-made is worse than no programme. You need to be able to take criticism, because everything you make gets pulled apart by the group on a Monday. And you need to be genuinely curious about people who are not like you – that one can't be taught, and it's the one that matters most.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: What sort of things do the volunteers make?

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: All sorts. One of them spent five months recording her grandfather's memories of arriving here in 1969, and made a documentary out of it. Another one runs a phone-in about school stress that gets more calls than anything else we do. A group of them made a comedy series about a fictional swimming pool, which sounds ridiculous and was genuinely funny. And two of our presenters now work in national radio.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: What's the hardest part of running it?

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: Money, obviously, but that's boring. The honest answer is letting go. When someone is about to make a programme in a way I think won't work, I have to say nothing. About half the time I'm right and it doesn't work, and they learn more from that than from me being right out loud.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Is there a moment you're most proud of?

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: There's one. Two years ago a girl called Ruth, who had barely spoken for the first six weeks she came, presented a live two-hour programme on her own when the person scheduled was ill. She was fifteen. Afterwards her mother rang me and couldn't finish the sentence she'd started. That's the whole thing, really. It was never about radio.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Tessa Iyer, thank you very much.

script.speaker: Tessa
script.text: Thank you.

questions.prompt: What was Tessa's job before she started the station?
questions.guidance: Ge 1 poäng för att hon var bibliotekarie. Godtagbart: ”a librarian”; ”she worked in a school library”.

scoreExamples.answer: She was a radio presenter.
She was a librarian.

questions.prompt: What did Tessa keep noticing about her students?
questions.guidance: Ge 1 poäng för svar som visar att de elever som hade mest att säga ofta var de som sa minst i klassrummet.

scoreExamples.answer: That they were not interested in maths.
That the students with the most to say often said the least in class.

questions.prompt: How did the station begin?
options: With money from the county council
With equipment the school was throwing out
With a grant from a national radio station
With a course Tessa took in 2017
questions.explanation: Skolan skulle slänga gammal inspelningsutrustning, och Tessa frågade om hon fick behålla den. Fyra personer började sedan göra ett halvtimmesprogram i ett tomt klassrum.

questions.prompt: How many listeners did they have during the first four months?
questions.guidance: Ge 1 poäng för elva. Godtagbart: ”eleven people”; ”11”. 0 poäng: ”nineteen thousand” (det är i dag).

scoreExamples.answer: Nineteen thousand.
Eleven.

questions.prompt: What does Tessa say made the biggest difference?
options: They stopped copying the radio they grew up with
They moved into a proper studio in the town centre
They began playing the music their parents had loved
They were given money by the school to buy equipment
questions.explanation: På frågan vad som förändrades svarar hon att de slutade försöka låta som den radio de vuxit upp med – och att allt blev bättre när de gjorde det.

questions.prompt: Who can join the station?
questions.guidance: Ge 1 poäng per led, max 2: den som är mellan fjorton och tjugoett år, och som bor i grevskapet (the county).

scoreExamples.answer: Anyone who wants to.
Anyone between fourteen and twenty-one.
Anyone between fourteen and twenty-one who lives in the county.

questions.prompt: To be part of the station, you need three things. What are they?
questions.guidance: Ge 1 poäng per led, max 3: 1) att dyka upp/passa tider (ett halvfärdigt program är sämre än inget), 2) att kunna ta kritik (allt granskas av gruppen på måndagar), 3) att vara genuint nyfiken på människor som inte är som en själv.

scoreExamples.answer: You need experience and a good radio voice.
You need to turn up.
You need to turn up and to be able to take criticism.
You need to turn up, to be able to take criticism from the group, and to be genuinely curious about people who are not like you.

questions.note: Du måste skriva alla tre för att få full poäng.

questions.prompt: What does Tessa say you do NOT need?
questions.explanation: Hon säger uttryckligen att man inte behöver det folk tänker på som en radioröst – de har medvetet gått bort från det. De övriga tre är sådant man just behöver.

questions.prompt: Mention two of the programmes the volunteers have made.
questions.guidance: Ge 1 poäng per korrekt exempel, max 2. I intervjun nämns: en dokumentär om en flickas farfar som kom hit 1969; ett telefonväktarprogram om skolstress; en komediserie om en påhittad simhall.

scoreExamples.answer: They make programmes about music.
A documentary about a girl's grandfather.
A documentary about a girl's grandfather arriving in 1969, and a phone-in programme about school stress.

questions.note: Du måste skriva två för att få full poäng.

questions.prompt: What does Tessa find hardest about running the station?
options: Finding enough new volunteers every September
Choosing which twenty people get a place each year
Staying quiet when she thinks someone is wrong
Working in the evenings and at weekends all year
questions.explanation: Hon nämner pengar men avfärdar det direkt som ”boring”, och säger att det ärliga svaret är att släppa taget: när någon är på väg att göra något hon tror inte fungerar måste hon tiga – och de lär sig mer av det än av att hon får rätt högt.

questions.prompt: What happened two years ago with the girl called Ruth?
questions.guidance: Ge 1 poäng per led, max 2: hon ledde ett direktsänt tvåtimmarsprogram helt själv när den inbokade personen blev sjuk, och hon var femton år – trots att hon knappt hade talat de första sex veckorna.

scoreExamples.answer: She started working in national radio.
She presented a live two-hour programme on her own.
She presented a live two-hour programme alone at fifteen, when the scheduled presenter was ill, even though she had barely spoken during her first six weeks.

questions.prompt: At the end Tessa says: ‘It was never about radio.' What does she mean?
questions.guidance: Ge upp till 3 poäng. 1 p: eleven förstår att radion inte är målet i sig. 2 p: eleven kopplar till exemplet med Ruth eller till hennes iakttagelse om eleverna som teg. 3 p: eleven formulerar att syftet är vad det gör med de unga – att de växer, tar plats och hittar sin röst – och att programmen bara är medlet.

scoreExamples.answer: She means that she is going to stop working with radio.
She means that the radio programmes are not the most important thing.
She means the point is what happens to the young people, like Ruth, who went from barely speaking to presenting two hours alone.

She means that the station exists for what it does to the people in it, not for the programmes. It goes back to what she noticed as a teacher – that those with most to say often said least – and Ruth is the proof: the radio is only the means by which someone finds their voice.

oral.delprov: Delprov A: speaking – Work and Money
oral.title: Work and Money

image.alt: Two young people talking at a table.

intro: På det muntliga delprovet samtalar ni två och två på engelska medan läraren lyssnar. Ni ska hjälpa varandra med frågor och kommentarer – det är ett samtal, inte två föredrag efter varandra.
I åk 9 räcker det inte att säga vad du tycker. Du ska förklara varför, ge exempel och gärna väga in att andra kan tycka annorlunda.
steps: Warm-up. Take turns to talk about: any job you have had or would like to have, whether you get pocket money and what you spend it on, and what you would do with a thousand kronor you were not expecting.
Part One. Take turns to pick a card. Read the three alternatives aloud and put the card on the table.
Say which alternative you would prefer, and explain why. Give an example.
Ask what your friend thinks – and why.
Then discuss together: which alternative do you think most people your age would choose, and which would your parents' generation choose? Why is there a difference, if there is one?
cards:
Which would you prefer?
• a job you love
• a job that pays very well
• a job with a lot of free time
Why? Ask your friend. What would most people choose?

Which would you prefer?
• working alone
• working in a small team
• leading a big group
Why? Ask your friend. What would most people choose?

Which would you prefer?
• saving your money
• spending it straight away
• giving some of it away
Why? Ask your friend. What would most people choose?

Which would you prefer?
• a summer job outdoors
• a summer job in a shop
• a summer job at home online
Why? Ask your friend. What would most people choose?

Which would you prefer?
• buying new
• buying second-hand
• repairing what you have
Why? Ask your friend. What would most people choose?

Which would you prefer?
• studying for many years
• starting work at eighteen
• starting your own business
Why? Ask your friend. What would most people choose?

Which would you prefer?
• being paid the same as everyone else
• being paid for what you produce
• being paid more for harder work
Why? Ask your friend. What would most people choose?

Which would you prefer?
• a famous job
• a useful job
• a well-paid job
Why? Ask your friend. What would most people choose?
assessmentPoints: Vi talade engelska hela tiden, även när det var svårt.
Jag utvecklade mina svar med skäl och exempel – inte bara ”I think it's good”.
Jag förklarade med andra ord när jag saknade ett ord, i stället för att byta till svenska.
Jag byggde vidare på det min kompis sa (”That's true, but …”, ”I hadn't thought of that”).
Jag ställde frågor tillbaka och höll samtalet igång.
Jag vågade tycka något annat än min kompis, och sa det på ett schysst sätt.
Vi turades om, så att vi båda fick ungefär lika mycket taltid.
Jag anpassade språket till situationen – det här är ett samtal, inte ett föredrag.

oral.delprov: Delprov A: speaking – Rules and Freedom
oral.title: Rules and Freedom
intro: Det här är ett andra muntligt delprov, i samma format men med påståenden i stället för valkort.
Ett påstående är till för att prövas. Du behöver inte bara hålla med eller inte hålla med – du kan säga ”it depends”, om du förklarar vad det beror på.
steps: Warm-up. Take turns to talk about: the rules you have at home, the rules you have at school, and one rule you think is unnecessary.
Part One. Take turns to pick a card and read the statement aloud. Put the card on the table.
Say whether you agree or disagree – and explain why, with an example.
Ask your friend what they think, and why.
If you disagree with each other, try to find out exactly where you start to disagree. If you agree, try to think of someone who would not, and explain their side.
cards:
Sixteen-year-olds should be allowed to vote.
Agree? Disagree? Explain why and give examples.
What does your friend think?

Schools should decide what pupils wear.
Agree? Disagree? Explain why and give examples.
What does your friend think?

Parents have the right to read their children's messages.
Agree? Disagree? Explain why and give examples.
What does your friend think?

Homework does more harm than good.
Agree? Disagree? Explain why and give examples.
What does your friend think?

It is better to be told the truth than to be protected from it.
Agree? Disagree? Explain why and give examples.
What does your friend think?

Everyone should have to do a year of work for the community after school.
Agree? Disagree? Explain why and give examples.
What does your friend think?

Some things should never be posted online, even if they are true.
Agree? Disagree? Explain why and give examples.
What does your friend think?

Young people today have more freedom than they can handle.
Agree? Disagree? Explain why and give examples.
What does your friend think?
